source_caption:
The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) is one of the most honest films ever made about what happens when soldiers come home from war.

Directed by William Wyler, the film follows three World War II veterans returning to Boone City, each carrying a different kind of wound. Al Stephenson (Fredric March) comes home to a loving family but struggles with alcohol, guilt, and the feeling that he no longer belongs in civilian life. Fred Derry (Dana Andrews), a decorated Air Force captain, discovers that his wartime heroism means very little when he returns to a struggling job market and a failing marriage. And Homer Parrish (Harold Russell) must face an even more difficult reality after losing both of his hands in the war.

What makes the film so powerful is that it never treats these men as simple heroes. They survived the war, but surviving doesn’t mean everything goes back to normal.

Russell’s performance is especially remarkable because he wasn’t a professional actor. He was a real World War II veteran who lost both hands in a training accident. He became the first non-professional actor to win an acting Oscar, taking home Best Supporting Actor for the role.

At the 1947 Academy Awards, the film won 7 Oscars from 8 nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director for William Wyler, Best Actor for Fredric March, Best Supporting Actor for Harold Russell, Best Screenplay, Best Film Editing, and Best Original Score. Russell also received an honorary Oscar for bringing hope and courage to disabled veterans through his performance.

It was also a huge audience success, becoming one of the highest-grossing films of its era.

Nearly 80 years later, The Best Years of Our Lives still feels remarkably human. It isn’t really a movie about war. It’s about what war leaves behind — and how difficult it can be to find your way home again.
